metadata.narrative: I help run a public library program for teens and adults, and people keep claiming that serious reading rewires empathy or that poetry is uniquely good for the brain. What should I actually believe? Can you help me understand what the research suggests about literary fiction, popular fiction, nonfiction, poetry, and group reading programs—especially which effects look short-term versus lasting, what kinds of brain responses have been observed, and what cautions I should keep in mind before designing a reading-for-wellbeing program?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A public library planning teen and adult reading programming should treat headline claims that literary fiction "rewires empathy" or that poetry is uniquely good for the brain as promising but unsettled hypotheses rather than proven facts.

The most influential experimental evidence is David Kidd and Emanuele Castano's study, which had participants read short excerpts of literary fiction, popular fiction, or nonfiction and then complete theory-of-mind tests such as the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test, finding that literary-fiction readers scored modestly higher, by roughly two questions out of thirty-six, than popular-fiction readers and controls.

That original finding has proven fragile: Maria Eugenia Panero and colleagues failed to replicate it, attributing the failure to the original study's very small effect sizes and noting there is no strong theoretical reason literary fiction specifically, rather than fiction generally, should boost theory of mind, since both genres deal in mental states.
A separate, larger-sample replication effort led by another research team also failed to reproduce the effect, disputing methodological details with the original authors along the way.

A broader synthesis of this literature concludes that several independent labs have now failed to replicate even the short-term, single-session version of the effect, while also cautioning that perspective-taking does not reliably make people kinder and can even increase unethical behavior in competitive situations.
Genre labels themselves are part of the problem: reviewers note the boundary between "literary" and "popular" fiction is fuzzy and historically unstable.

Empirical attempts to test literariness directly have produced inconsistent results, with some studies finding only romance and thriller genres predict mentalizing ability and others replicating Kidd and Castano's literary-only pattern, and even a recent replication attempt by Kidd and Castano's own group reported mixed findings.

A large registered longitudinal study using Germany's National Educational Panel Study dataset adds an important corrective: cross-sectional correlational meta-analyses show fiction reading correlates with self-reported empathy (r = 0.07), fantasy engagement (r = 0.18), and theory-of-mind performance (r = 0.21), all modest, with nonfiction correlations weaker still, and such correlations cannot establish that reading causes the outcome rather than empathic people simply preferring fiction.

That same longitudinal study distinguishes single-session experiments, which capture only immediate, possibly transient priming effects, from genuinely cumulative exposure across school years, and found that cumulative reading of "modern classic literature" specifically predicted later prosocial behavior and social adjustment in adolescents, while cumulative popular fiction, nonfiction, and comics did not.

A large-scale meta-analysis combining seventy experimental studies and additional correlational studies, involving more than eleven thousand participants, confirms the pattern that fiction produces small but statistically significant cognitive benefits, most pronounced for empathy and theory of mind in experiments and for verbal and general cognitive ability in lifetime-exposure correlations, with fiction's advantage clearer relative to nonfiction than relative to doing nothing.

The same meta-analysis raises a crucial interpretive caution for program design: because short single-session experiments show only priming-sized effects on social cognition, while lifetime correlational studies show effects concentrated in verbal and general cognitive skills, it remains genuinely unclear whether reading fiction causes durable psychological change or whether people with strong verbal and social skills are simply the ones who read more fiction.

On the specific question of short-term versus lasting effects, controlled experiments by Bal and Veltkamp are directly relevant: empathy did not shift immediately after participants finished a story, but changed over roughly a one-week delay, a pattern the researchers describe as an "absolute sleeper effect."

This delayed change occurred only among readers who reported strong emotional transportation into the narrative, with low-transportation readers actually showing decreased empathy and nonfiction-control readers showing no such shift at all.

A related experimental study adds a further nuance about individual differences: readers low in the personality trait Openness who read a short story showed a measurable increase in self-reported cognitive empathy but no corresponding increase in affective empathy, showing positive effects can be uneven across empathy's components and across readers.

Turning to poetry, the clearest neuroscience evidence available is a University of Exeter fMRI study comparing brain responses to prose, sonnets, and each participant's favorite poems, which found a general "reading network" activated by any text but showed poetry specifically engaged the posterior cingulate cortex and medial temporal lobes, regions linked to introspection.

Favorite poems activated memory-related regions more strongly than ordinary reading areas, suggesting a recollection-like process, but the study used only thirteen volunteers, all English-faculty members or graduate students, so it should be treated as a preliminary signal rather than proof that poetry as a genre is uniquely good for a general public's brain.

Where the evidence looks considerably stronger and more directly actionable for library programming is structured group reading rather than any single genre's neural effects: an evaluation of the Kirklees "Well into Words" bibliotherapy project found that facilitated reading groups improved participants' mental health, motivation, confidence, and social inclusion, and identified five concrete success factors, namely the literature chosen, facilitator skill, partnership working, the physical environment, and group dynamics.

The Reading Agency's Reading Friends program, designed for isolated older adults, reported that 88 percent of participants felt the program increased valuable social contact and gave purpose to their week, prompting a recommendation that health systems fund book-based social prescribing through libraries.

An Oxford-led review of library-based lifelong-learning programs offers a design framework independent of any single book's content, identifying libraries as "therapeutic landscapes" through their welcoming, low-pressure, non-commercial atmosphere, describing how absorbing activities can produce a restorative sense of "flow," and emphasizing that structure, purpose, reminiscence, and social engagement are the recurring mechanisms behind measured wellbeing gains.

Combining these strands, a defensible working position for program design is that fiction, especially when it emotionally absorbs readers, has modest correlational and experimental support for empathy-related benefits that may take time to appear rather than showing up immediately.

"Literary" superiority over popular fiction is empirically contested and inconsistently replicated, nonfiction shows weaker but nonzero associations with social-cognitive outcomes, and poetry's distinctive brain signature rests on very limited preliminary imaging data.

The most robust, least disputed benefits come from well-facilitated group reading itself, through social connection, structure, and a welcoming library environment, rather than from any specific text reliably rewiring readers' brains.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

output.text:
A public library considering a reading-for-wellbeing program should treat claims that literary fiction "rewires empathy" or that poetry is uniquely good for the brain as promising but contested hypotheses rather than settled science.

The most famous evidence comes from David Kidd and Emanuele Castano's 2013 Science study, which ran five experiments giving readers short excerpts of literary fiction, popular fiction, or nonfiction and then measured theory-of-mind performance on tests like the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test.

Literary-fiction readers modestly outperformed popular-fiction readers and controls, but the actual size of the difference was small, roughly two extra correct answers out of thirty-six, even though outside commentators argued small effects can still matter if they translate into fewer real-world social misunderstandings.

That original finding has not held up consistently: Maria Eugenia Panero and colleagues failed to replicate it in 2016, arguing the original effect sizes were simply too small to be robust and that both literary and popular fiction are "about mental states," giving no strong theoretical reason to expect literary fiction alone to boost theory of mind.

A separate, larger-sample replication attempt by a Goldstein-led team also failed to reproduce the effect, and although Kidd and Castano disputed the quality controls used, several independent labs contributing to that null result had found the same thing before even knowing about each other's work.

A broader synthesis piece notes this pattern directly: multiple labs have failed to replicate even the short-term, single-session effects of literary fiction on perspective-taking, and cautions that taking another person's perspective does not reliably make people behave better and can even increase competitive unethical behavior or negative views of perceived threats.

Kidd and Castano's own later follow-up work found their pattern replicated across three samples using an author-recognition measure of literary exposure, but the researchers themselves flagged an important caution: performance on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test is entangled with verbal IQ, not cleanly isolated cognitive empathy, and they explicitly retreated from claiming literary fiction is "superior" to other genres.

Other empirical work complicates the story further: one large convenience-sample study found that overall fiction exposure did not significantly predict empathy scores at all, while the frequency or regularity of reading did, suggesting habit and dosage may matter more than genre "literariness."

On the question of short-term versus lasting effects, Matthijs Bal and Martijn Veltkamp's controlled experiments are especially informative for a librarian designing programming: empathy did not shift immediately after reading, but changed over roughly a one-week window, and only among readers who reported strong emotional "transportation" into the story.

Low-transportation fiction readers in that study actually showed decreased empathy, and readers assigned to a nonfiction control condition showed no such delayed shift in either direction, indicating that emotional immersion, not genre label alone, is the operative mechanism and that effects can be a delayed "sleeper effect" rather than instant.

A large registered longitudinal study using Germany's National Educational Panel Study dataset adds important nuance about durability: cross-sectional correlational studies show fiction reading correlated with empathy, fantasy involvement, and theory-of-mind performance more strongly than nonfiction reading, but these correlations are modest and cannot establish causation because highly empathic people may simply be drawn to fiction.

That same study distinguishes single-session experiments, which only capture short-term priming-like effects, from genuinely longitudinal designs, and found that cumulative exposure specifically to "modern classic literature" across school grades predicted later prosocial behavior and social adjustment, while cumulative popular fiction, nonfiction, and comics did not show this effect.

Turning to nonfiction specifically, the evidence gathered here suggests it is not without cognitive value but is consistently associated with weaker empathy- and theory-of-mind-related correlations than fiction, and in controlled experiments it does not appear to move empathy scores up or down the way emotionally transporting fiction can.

On poetry and the brain, the clearest neuroimaging evidence available comes from a University of Exeter fMRI study led by Adam Zeman, which compared brain responses to prose, sonnets, and each participant's favorite poems in a small sample of thirteen English-faculty volunteers and graduate students.

That study found a general "reading network" activated by any written material, but poetry specifically activated regions such as the posterior cingulate cortex and medial temporal lobes linked to introspection and memory, and favorite poems activated memory regions more strongly than ordinary "reading" regions, suggesting a recollection-like process; given the tiny, highly literate sample, this should be read as an intriguing preliminary finding rather than proof that poetry is uniquely good for a general public's brain.

For group reading programs specifically, the evidence is more encouraging and more directly relevant to library practice: an evaluation of the Kirklees "Well into Words" bibliotherapy project found that structured reading groups improved participants' mental health, motivation, confidence, and social inclusion, and identified five concrete drivers of success, namely the literature selected, facilitator skill, partnership working, the physical environment, and group dynamics.

The Reading Agency's Reading Friends program, aimed at isolated and lonely older adults, reported that 88 percent of participants felt the program increased valuable social contact and gave purpose to their week, supporting calls for treating shared reading as a social-prescribing tool rather than only a cognitive intervention.

A related Oxford review of library-based lifelong-learning programs identifies mechanisms that likely explain why such groups help even without proven neural rewiring: libraries function as low-pressure "therapeutic landscapes," structured activities can induce a restorative sense of "flow," and group participation builds social capital, all independent of whether any single book changes a reader's brain.

Taken together, a defensible position for program design is that emotionally immersive fiction, read regularly and reflected upon, has correlational and modest experimental support for empathy-related benefits, that these effects are more consistent when measured over time than immediately after a single session, that "literary versus popular" distinctions are less robust and more disputed than headlines suggest, that poetry's brain effects rest on very small preliminary neuroimaging samples, and that the strongest, least contested evidence favors well-facilitated group reading for social connection and wellbeing rather than any single genre's power to reshape empathy on its own.

output.text:
A public library planning teen and adult reading programming should treat headline claims that literary fiction "rewires empathy" or that poetry is uniquely good for the brain as promising but unsettled hypotheses rather than proven facts.

The most influential experimental evidence is David Kidd and Emanuele Castano's study, which had participants read short excerpts of literary fiction, popular fiction, or nonfiction and then complete theory-of-mind tests such as the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test, finding that literary-fiction readers scored modestly higher, by roughly two questions out of thirty-six, than popular-fiction readers and controls.

That original finding has proven fragile: Maria Eugenia Panero and colleagues failed to replicate it, attributing the failure to the original study's very small effect sizes and noting there is no strong theoretical reason literary fiction specifically, rather than fiction generally, should boost theory of mind, since both genres deal in mental states.

A separate, larger-sample replication effort led by another research team also failed to reproduce the effect, and a broader synthesis of this literature concludes that several independent labs have now failed to replicate even the short-term, single-session version of the effect, while also cautioning that perspective-taking does not reliably make people kinder and can even increase unethical behavior in competitive situations.

Genre labels themselves are part of the problem: reviewers note the boundary between "literary" and "popular" fiction is fuzzy and historically unstable, and empirical attempts to test literariness directly have produced inconsistent results, with some studies finding only romance and thriller genres predict mentalizing ability and others replicating Kidd and Castano's literary-only pattern.

A large registered longitudinal study using Germany's National Educational Panel Study dataset adds an important corrective: cross-sectional correlational meta-analyses show fiction reading correlates with empathy (r = 0.07), fantasy engagement (r = 0.18), and theory-of-mind performance (r = 0.21), all modest, with nonfiction correlations weaker still, and these correlations cannot establish that reading causes the outcome rather than empathic people simply preferring fiction.

That same longitudinal study distinguishes single-session experiments, which capture only immediate, possibly transient priming effects, from genuinely cumulative exposure across school years, and found that cumulative reading of "modern classic literature" specifically predicted later prosocial behavior and social adjustment in adolescents, while cumulative popular fiction, nonfiction, and comics did not.

A large-scale meta-analysis combining seventy experimental studies and additional correlational studies, involving more than eleven thousand participants, confirms the pattern that fiction produces small but statistically significant cognitive benefits, most pronounced for empathy and theory of mind in experiments and for verbal and general cognitive ability in lifetime-exposure correlations, and importantly finds fiction's advantage is clearer relative to nonfiction than relative to doing nothing.

The same meta-analysis raises a crucial interpretive caution for program design: because short single-session experiments show only priming-sized effects on social cognition, while lifetime correlational studies show effects concentrated in verbal and general cognitive skills, it remains genuinely unclear whether reading fiction causes durable psychological change or whether people with strong verbal and social skills are simply the ones who read more fiction.

On the specific question of short-term versus lasting effects, controlled experiments by Bal and Veltkamp are directly relevant: empathy did not shift immediately after participants finished a story, but changed over roughly a one-week delay, a pattern the researchers describe as an "absolute sleeper effect," and this delayed change occurred only among readers who reported strong emotional transportation into the narrative, with low-transportation readers actually showing decreased empathy and nonfiction-control readers showing no such shift at all.

A related experimental study adds a further nuance about individual differences: readers low in the personality trait Openness who read a short story showed a measurable increase in self-reported cognitive empathy but no corresponding increase in affective empathy, indicating that even positive effects can be uneven across empathy's cognitive and emotional components and across different kinds of readers.

Turning to poetry, the clearest neuroscience evidence available is a University of Exeter fMRI study comparing brain responses to prose, sonnets, and each participant's favorite poems, which found a general "reading network" activated by any text but showed poetry specifically engaged the posterior cingulate cortex and medial temporal lobes, regions linked to introspection, while favorite poems activated memory-related regions more strongly than ordinary reading areas, suggesting a recollection-like process.

That study used only thirteen volunteers, all English-faculty members or graduate students, so it should be treated as an intriguing preliminary signal about emotionally resonant, familiar poetry rather than proof that poetry as a genre is uniquely good for a general public's brain.

Where the evidence looks considerably stronger and more directly actionable for library programming is structured group reading rather than any single genre's neural effects: an evaluation of the Kirklees "Well into Words" bibliotherapy project found that facilitated reading groups improved participants' mental health, motivation, confidence, and social inclusion, and identified five concrete success factors, namely the literature chosen, facilitator skill, partnership working, the physical environment, and group dynamics.

The Reading Agency's Reading Friends program, designed for isolated older adults, reported that 88 percent of participants felt the program increased valuable social contact and gave purpose to their week, prompting a recommendation that health systems fund book-based social prescribing through libraries.

An Oxford-led review of library-based lifelong-learning programs offers a useful design framework independent of any single book's content, identifying libraries as "therapeutic landscapes" through their welcoming, low-pressure, non-commercial atmosphere, describing how absorbing activities can produce a restorative sense of "flow," and emphasizing that structure, purpose, reminiscence, and above all social engagement are the recurring mechanisms behind measured wellbeing gains.

Combining these strands, a defensible working position for program design is that fiction, especially when it emotionally absorbs readers, has modest correlational and experimental support for empathy-related benefits that may take time to appear rather than showing up immediately, that "literary" superiority over popular fiction is empirically contested and inconsistently replicated, that nonfiction shows weaker but nonzero associations with social-cognitive outcomes, that poetry's distinctive brain signature rests on very limited preliminary imaging data, and that the most robust, least disputed benefits come from well-facilitated group reading itself, through social connection, structure, and a welcoming library environment, rather than from any specific text reliably rewiring readers' brains.

answer.text: A public library planning teen and adult reading programming should treat headline claims that literary fiction "rewires empathy" or that poetry is uniquely good for the brain as promising but unsettled hypotheses rather than proven facts.

A separate, larger-sample replication effort led by another research team also failed to reproduce the effect, disputing methodological details with the original authors along the way.

A broader synthesis of this literature concludes that several independent labs have now failed to replicate even the short-term, single-session version of the effect, while also cautioning that perspective-taking does not reliably make people kinder and can even increase unethical behavior in competitive situations.
Genre labels themselves are part of the problem: reviewers note the boundary between "literary" and "popular" fiction is fuzzy and historically unstable.

Empirical attempts to test literariness directly have produced inconsistent results, with some studies finding only romance and thriller genres predict mentalizing ability and others replicating Kidd and Castano's literary-only pattern, and even a recent replication attempt by Kidd and Castano's own group reported mixed findings.
